Abstract 
Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables direct computation on encrypted data without decryption, ensuring 
data privacy in cloud computing scenarios and preventing the leakage of sensitive information. However, the compu-
tational overhead of HE typically exceeds that of plaintext computation by 4 to 5 orders of magnitude, while energy 
consumption is 5 to 6 orders of magnitude higher. These substantial performance and energy overheads significantly 
hinder the widespread adoption of FHE. This paper proposed LP-HENN, a novel low-power and energy-efficient FHE 
accelerator architecture that leverages a RISC-V vector coprocessor and ReRAM crossbar arrays. LP-HENN targets 
power-constrained application scenarios such as edge devices, aiming to provide highly energy-efficient acceleration 
support for FHE applications. LP-HENN leverages the collaborative work of the vector processor and ReRAM cross-
bars, employing optimization strategies to achieve full pipelining and minimize memory access. Furthermore, this 
paper proposed a parameter selection model for early-stage architecture design, which achieves an optimal balance 
between performance and energy consumption through the collaborative optimization of multiple parameters. 
Experimental results show that, for an FHE-based convolutional neural network (HE-CNN) inference application, LP-
HENN achieves a 31.82Ã- and 11920.56Ã- improvement in performance and energy efficiency, respectively, compared 
to CPU. Compared to FxHENN, the state-of-the-art FPGA-based FHE accelerator with high energy efficiency for edge 
devices, LP-HENN achieves a 2.36Ã- and 10.04Ã- improvement in performance and energy efficiency, respectively. The 
energy efficiency of LP-HENN is comparable to that of F1, the state-of-the-art ASIC FHE accelerator, while featuring 
a low power design suitable for edge computing.

Introduction
Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) is a special type 
of encryption scheme that enables direct computations 
on encrypted data without requiring decryption. The 
encrypted result of these computations, when decrypted, 
yields an output identical to that obtained from perform-
ing the same computations on the original plaintext data. 
This capability facilitates the development of applications 
with end-to-end encrypted data processing, ensuring 
data security even in untrusted environments, as Fig. 1” 
illustrates.
Despite the tremendous potential of FHE, its sig-
nificant overhead makes it challenging to be widely 
adopted in the real world. Currently, even with state-
of-the-art FHE libraries (Chen et  al. 2017; Al  Badawi 
et al. 2022; Mouchet et al. 2020), homomorphic encryp-
tion computations on CPUs are 4-5 orders of mag-
nitude slower than their plaintext counterparts. This 
enormous computational overhead not only reduces

To reduce the performance and energy consumption 
overheads of FHE, researchers have conducted exten-
sive studies and proposed a series of FHE hardware 
accelerators ( Samardzic et  al. 2021; Samardzic et  al. 
2022; Kim et al. 2022a; b; Agrawal et al. 2023; Yang et al. 
2023; Kim et al. 2023; Zhu et al. 2023). In the domain 
of edge computing, FxHENN (Zhu et  al. 2023) is the 
first FPGA FHE accelerator supporting comprehensive 
end-to-end neural network applications. Compared to 
CPUs, FxHENN achieves a speedup of 13.49Ã- and an 
energy efficiency improvement of 1187.12Ã-.
FHE operations process long vectors (typically rang-
ing from 16384 to 65536 elements in length), with 
the most of computations being element-wise opera-
tions on these vectors, thus exhibiting a high degree 
of data-level parallelism (DLP). Futhermore, FHE 
programs do not involve any branches, making them 
highly suitable for processing with vector processors. 
Vector processors are characterized by their superior 
energy efficiency while providing ample computational 
capability for applications with high DLP. Given the 
deterministic nature of the computation process, com-
putation and memory access can be effectively over-
lapped with an appropriate scheduling strategy.
The extensive use of Number Theoretic Transform 
(NTT) in FHE introduces significant computational 
and memory access overhead, making it the primary 
performance bottleneck. Therefore, to improve the per-
formance of FHE, the incorporation of additional mod-
ules dedicated to accelerating NTT computations is 
necessary. Prior research has demonstrated that Num-
ber Theoretic Transform (NTT) computations can be 
efficiently expressed using matrix operations (Fan et al. 
2023). Resistive Random Access Memory (ReRAM) 
crossbar arrays excel at matrix–vector multiplication 
with high energy efficiency (Shafiee et al. 2016; Liu et al. 
2022), as they can perform hundreds of parallel vector 
dot products. Furthermore, previous studies (Park et al. 
2022) have demonstrated that ReRAM-based NTT com-
putations not only achieve superior energy efficiency 
(12.7% lower energy consumption) but also significantly 
higher throughput (63.8Ã-) compared to ASIC imple-
mentations. Thus, leveraging ReRAM crossbar arrays for 
NTT acceleration emerges as a promising approach.
Based on these observations, this paper proposed LP-
HENN, a highly energy-efficient architecture for FHE 
in edge computing scenarios. LP-HENN integrates a 
RISC-V vector coprocessor and ReRAM crossbar arrays 
to achieve high energy efficiency. The design of FHE 
accelerators involves numerous software and hardware 
parameters. The values of these parameters and their 
combinations profoundly influence the performance 
and energy efficiency of FHE accelerators. For example, 
unneccesary large parameters can unnecessari increase 
computational overhead and cause bad performance and 
high energy consumption. To choose the optimal soft-
ware and hardware parameters in the early architectural 
design stage, we provide a parameter selection model.
Experimental results show that for the LoLa-CIFAR 
(Brutzkus et  al. 2019) HE-CNN application, LP-HENN 
achieves a speedup of 31.82Ã- and an energy efficiency 
improvement of 11920.56Ã- compared to CPUs. Com-
pared to FxHENN, LP-HENN achieves a speedup of 
2.36Ã- and an energy efficiency improvement of 10.04Ã-.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:
•	 We present LP-HENN, a novel architecture that 
combines a RISC-V vector coprocessor with ReRAM

•	 We develop a parameter selection model for LP-

design to balance the accelerator’s performance and

•	 We evaluate the performance and power consump-
tion of LP-HENN using the LoLa (Brutzkus et  al.

demonstrate significant improvements in both per-

Background
The LP-HENN architecture is applicable to FHE schemes 
such as BGV (Brakerski et al. 2014), BFV (Fan and Ver-
cauteren 2012), and CKKS (Cheon et al. 2017), as their 
computations are similar. This paper focuses on CKKS 
over other popular homomorphic encryption schemes 
(BFV, BGV, and TFHE) for the following reasons:
•	 The CKKS scheme efficiently supports the encryp-
tion of fixed-point complex vectors and currently 
stands as the most efficient scheme for performing 
approximate homomorphic computations over real 
and complex numbers (Kim et al. 2022). This makes 
it particularly suitable for machine learning (ML) 
applications. In contrast, BFV and BGV schemes 
are designed for exact computations with integer 
data types, while TFHE operates on bits. Applying 
these alternative schemes to ML workloads requires 
quantization, and they lack efficient mechanisms for 
rounding real numbers, limiting their practicality for 
ML applications.
•	 While BFV and BGV support SIMD-style ciphertext 
packing (allowing multiple numbers in one cipher-
text), their packing efficiency is substantially lower 
than CKKS (Badawi and Polyakov 2023). Due to 
their message encoding methodology, BFV and BGV 
restrict SIMD-encoded vectors to sizes of 2K or less, 
whereas CKKS supports vector sizes ranging from 
32K to 64K. Consequently, BGV and BFV computa-
tions achieve significantly lower throughput com-
pared to CKKS.

Hierarchical description of RNS‑CKKS
From a computational perspective, an FHE application 
built on the CKKS scheme can be divided into the follow-
ing four layers:
•	 Application layer: Applications constructed upon 
the CKKS scheme, such as convolutional neural net-
works (CNNs) (Lee et al. 2022) and logistic regres-
sion (Han et al. 2019).
•	 FHE primitive layer: FHE primitive operations 
described in Sect. “CKKS scheme”, including HAdd, 
HMult, HRotate, PMult, PAdd, and Rescale.
•	 FHE Operator layer: The operators that compose the 
primitives operations, including ModUp, ModDown, 
KeySwitch, BConv, DComp, and InnerProd-
uct.
•	 Vector operation layer: The various FHE operators 
are composed of the following basic vector opera-
tions: vector modular addition (VecAddMod), vector 
modular subtraction (VecSubMod), vector modular 
multiplication (VecMulMod), vector modulo (Vec-
Mod), vector addition (VecAdd), vector multiplica-
tion (VecMul), automorphism, and (I)NTT.

Matrix–vector multiplication accelerator based on ReRAM 
crossbars
The matrix–vector multiplication accelerator based on 
ReRAM crossbars is illustrated in Fig.  3. The accelera-
tor comprises ReRAM crossbars, digital-to-analog con-
verters (DACs), analog-to-digital converters (ADCs), 
sample-and-hold (S&H) circuits, shifters, and adders, 
which work in concert to facilitate efficient matrix–vec-
tor multiplication.
ReRAM crossbars perform matrix–vector multipli-
cation in the analog domain. The input vector is con-
verted into voltages V0, V1, . . . , Vm−1 via DACs to drive 
the cells on the corresponding wordlines. Let the con-
ductances of the cells in a single column of the crossbar 
be G0, G1, . . . , Gm−1 . According to Kirchhoff’s law, the 
output current on the bitline is m−1
i=0 ViGi , thus com-
pleting the dot product operation between the input 
vector (V0, V1, . . . , Vm−1) and the conductance vector 
(G0, G1, . . . , Gm−1) . Subsequently, the S&H circuit sam-
ples the bitline current and forwards it to the ADC to 
convert the analog current signal into a digital signal. As 
a number may be distributed across multiple cells, the 
output result of each bitline corresponds to a partial sum. 
These partial sums are then accumulated using shifters 
and adders to obtain the final dot product result. The col-
umns of the crossbar array operate in parallel, enabling 
an mÃ-n crossbar array to simultaneously compute n dot 
products of vectors with length m, thereby achieving a 
high degree of parallelism. This architecture serves as a 
low-power, high-efficiency dot product engine, making it 
well-suited for matrix–vector multiplication tasks.
Practical applications and significance
This research on low-power homomorphic encryption 
accelerators for edge computing presents significant 
practical applications.
Scenario 1: Edge computing-based facial recognition 
systems with homomorphic encryption. While facial rec-
ognition technology has been widely deployed, particu-
larly in security systems for suspect detection, traditional 
face recognition systems face two major challenges. First, 
processing large crowds creates substantial computa-
tional and storage overhead for central servers. Offload-
ing these computations to edge devices can significantly 
reduce the data center burden. Second, protecting the 
security of feature vector databases is crucial, as directly 
storing facial feature vectors can compromise both user 
privacy and system security (Naresh Boddeti 2018). Edge 
homomorphic accelerators effectively address both chal-
lenges by storing encrypted feature vector databases on 
edge devices and computing Euclidean distances (or sim-
ilar matching metrics) between plaintext input data and 
encrypted database vectors. The encrypted results are 
then transmitted to central servers for decryption and 
match determination. This approach distributes com-
putational and storage loads while ensuring database 
security through encryption. However, homomorphic 
encryption operations are computationally intensive, 
leading to high latency on conventional hardware. There-
fore, specialized accelerators are necessary to achieve 
acceptable latency levels.

Motivation
To understand the challenges faced in the low-power 
FHE accelerators, this section presents an in-depth anal-
ysis of the characteristics of FHE applications from the 
perspectives of energy consumption, memory access, and 
parameter selection, based on the HE-CNN applications 
LoLa-MNIST and LoLa-CIFAR(Brutzkus et  al. 2019). 
The results indicate that the NTT is the primary bot-
tleneck, dominating both performance and energy con-
sumption. Additionally, the selection of parameters in the 
CKKS scheme and the architectural design strongly influ-
ences the performance, energy efficiency, and resource 
utilization of FHE accelerators. The potential optimiza-
tion opportunities derived from these findings are then 
summarized.
Energy and performance implications of NTT in FHE

Our first observation is that NTT operations constitute 
the primary bottleneck in terms of both energy consump-
tion and computational performance, making their opti-
mization crucial for advancing FHE accelerator designs.
From an energy consumption perspective, our analy-

significant findings. As shown in Fig. 4, NTT computa-

while its associated memory access operations account 
for an additional 27.4%. The implementation utilizes the 
Cooley-Tukey butterfly algorithm for (I)NTT operations, 
with experimental configuration detailed in Table 4. Even 
in F1(Samardzic et  al. 2021), a state-of-the-art ASIC 
implementation of FHE featuring highly optimized NTT 
units, these units still constitute 42.7% of the total energy

previous results are obtained, and subsequent computa-
tions can only be initiated upon the completion of NTT. 
Consequently, NTT is the primary performance bottle-
neck in FHE applications. This finding aligns with previ-
ous research (Fan et al. 2023), which demonstrates that 
NTT operations dominate the overall runtime, account-
ing for more than 90% across all benchmarks. The sub-
optimal performance of NTT can be primarily attributed 
to the strict data dependencies between the stages of the 
Cooley-Tukey butterfly algorithm. Each stage must wait 
for the previous stage to complete its computation, write 
the results back to memory, and then read the results 
written by the previous stage before proceeding with its 
own computation. All log2 N stages require all N ele-
ments to be read and written once, resulting in a signifi-
cant amount of memory access. Furthermore, the strict 
data dependencies prevent any overlap between the com-
putation time and memory access time in NTT, exacer-
bating the performance bottleneck.
Therefore, optimizing both performance and energy 
efficiency of NTT operations is crucial for enhancing 
FHE accelerator designs. ReRAM crossbar architecture 
presents a promising opportunity by enabling NTT com-
putation through matrix–vector multiplication, offering 
high parallelism and significantly reduced data depend-
encies. Under the same manufacturing process node, this 
approach demonstrates 40% lower energy consumption 
compared to F1 (Park et al. 2022; Samardzic et al. 2021).
Parameter selection
The design of FHE accelerators involves numerous soft-
ware and hardware parameters, which collectively con-
stitute a large parameter space. The software parameters 
are the parameters of the CKKS scheme, including the 
number of polynomial terms ( N ), the initial level of 
ciphertexts ( L ), the decomposition number ( dnum ) in 
KeySwitch , and the bit length of the small primes ( qj ) 
( B ). The hardware parameters include the size of the on-
chip cache, the capacity of the Dynamic Random-Access 
Memory (DRAM), and the number of functional units.
The values of these parameters and their combina-
tions profoundly influence the performance and energy 
efficiency of FHE accelerators. The computational over-
head of homomorphic operations is proportional to N . 
For example, when N = 16384 , the computational cost 
of homomorphic operations is twice that of N = 8192 . 
However, N also impacts the security level, and a small 
N may fail to satisfy the security requirements. Fur-
thermore, N determines the vector length in FHE 
applications, and different values of N lead to a vary-
ing number of primitive operations. The computational 
overhead of primitive operations is proportional to ℓ ,

Opportunities
Based on the above observations, we identify the follow-
ing opportunities to improve the energy efficiency of FHE 
accelerators:
•	 From the perspectives of latency, computational 
overhead, memory access, and power consumption, 
NTT is the primary bottleneck in FHE applications. 
Consequently, optimizing (I)NTT will have a sig-
nificant impact on the performance and power con-
sumption of FHE accelerators. Previous studies (Park 
et  al. 2022) have demonstrated that ReRAM-based 
NTT computations not only achieve superior energy 
efficiency (12.7% lower energy consumption) but also 
significantly higher throughput (63.8Ã-) compared 
to ASIC implementations. Therefore, leveraging 
ReRAM crossbars to perform NTT may substantially 
improve both the performance and energy efficiency 
of FHE accelerators. Furthermore, The operators that 
constitute FHE applications can be converted into 
vector operations. Given the superior energy effi-
ciency of vector processors, they present a compel-
ling option for implementing most FHE operators.
•	 The selection of parameters in the CKKS scheme and 
the architectural design profoundly impacts the per-
formance, energy efficiency, and resource utilization 
of FHE accelerators. However, the huge parameter 
search space and complex interdepencies between 
these parameters make manual parameter selection a 
challenging task. Consequently, an automatic param-
eter selection model is essential for design of FHE 
accelerators.

architecture and a parameter selection model to optimize 
energy efficiency. In the following sections, we will pre-

model in detail.

Figure 6 illustrates the architecture of Ara, which col-
laborates with the CVA6 (Zaruba and Benini 2019), a 
RISC-V 64-bit scalar processor. Ara consists of a main 
sequencer, a slide unit (SLDU), a vector load/store unit 
(VLSU), and multiple lanes. The main sequencer moni-
tors vector instructions running on Ara, dispatches vec-
tor instructions to execution units, and acknowledges 
with CVA6. The SLDU handles instructions that require 
access to the vector register files (VRF) across multiple 
lanes, such as vector slide instructions like vslideup 
and vector register gather instructions like vrgather. 
The VLSU performs data transfers via an AXI interface 
and supports unit-stride, constant-stride, and indexed 
load and store instructions. The addresses of unit-stride 
memory instructions are merged to reduce the number 
of memory requests. Lanes serve as the primary execu-
tion units, with each lane containing an Arithmetic 
Logic Unit (ALU), a Floating Point Unit (FPU), an inte-
ger multiplier (MUL), and a portion of the VRF. These 
three execution units have the same throughput of 64 
bits/cycle, supporting 1 64-bit operation, 2 32-bit opera-
tions, 4 16-bit operations, or 8 8-bit operations per cycle. 
The VRF within each lane comprises eight single-ported 
banks with a width of 64 bits. Ara is scalable, supporting 
different configurations of the number of lanes l , which 
can be set to 2, 4, 8, or 16.
Ara makes modifications to CVA6. During the decod-
ing stage, CVA6 dispatches vector instructions to Ara. 
Upon confirming that the instructions will not trig-
ger exceptions, Ara sends an acknowledgment signal to 
CVA6 through the sequencer. Then Ara executes instruc-
tions sequentially without speculation. As FHE applica-
tions exhibit completely deterministic behavior and do 
not require branch instructions, sequential execution 
does not incur performance loss. Multiple lanes execute 
a vector instruction simultaneously. Since FHE operators 
do not involve instructions that require handling by the 
SLDU, and each lane has an independent VRF storing a 
portion of the vector operands, execution across lanes is 
relatively independent.

Chunk&fusion optimization
Performance of FHE accelerators is often constrained 
by memory bandwidth (Kim et  al. 2022a). Minimizing 
data movement between the cache and SPM, as well as 
between the VRF and cache, significantly impacts the 
performance of LP-HENN. This section proposes the 
chunk&fusion optimization to reduce data movement 
and enhance performance.
Fusion refers to the thorough integration of computa-
tions within the same FHE primitive operation, ensuring 
that after reading data, as much computation as possible 
is performed to eliminate all unnecessary write-after-
read operations.
According to Sect.  “Vector unit: structure and work-
flow”, due to the limitation of VLEN, the maximum vec-
tor operand length supported by the vector unit is much 
smaller than the vector length in FHE applications. The 
VLEN of Ara when #channels=16 is 16384 bits. In con-
trast, when B = 30, N = 8192 , the size of one limb is 
32768 bytes. Even with an LMUL of 8, a single vector

to compute NTT”) elements of a limb at a time, referred

Due to the limited capacity of the VRF, vector regis-

quent computations. There are three cases for releasing 
a chunk: 
1.	 The chunk is no longer required for subsequent com-
putations.
2.	 The chunk is needed for subsequent computations, 
but due to the VRF capacity limitation, it cannot be 
stored until the next use. In this case, it needs to be 
written back to the SPM, and the vector register is 
released.
3.	 NTTU (Sect.  “NTT Unit”) requires the chunk as 
input. In this case, it needs to be written back to the 
SPM for NTTU to read. The vector register should 
be released because the computations after NTT will 
not use the original chunk data but rather the output 
of NTT.

together). However, the vector registers cannot hold

Adjustment 1: Storing only 1 bit per cell to avoid errors 
The resistances of ReRAM are susceptible to random 
offsets and discrepancies from the target resistances 
due to the manufacturing process and the underly-
ing electrochemical mechanisms. Even within the same 
device, resistances may exhibit slight variations across 
different cycles, which can result in current errors dur-
ing dot product computations. If the current error 
exceeds the ADC resolution, the dot product calcula-
tion results will be erroneous. Unlike neural network 
accelerators that exhibit tolerance to errors (Shafiee et al. 
2016), NTT mandates strict accuracy. For example, let

of crossbar computations.

multi-level cell (MLC) requires the use of more com-

Automatic parameter selection model
Overview
The design of FHE accelerators involves numerous 
software and hardware parameters, which collec-
tively constitute a large parameter space. The software 
parameters are the parameters of the CKKS scheme, 
including the number of polynomial terms ( N ), the ini-
tial level of ciphertexts ( L ), the decomposition number 
( dnum ) in KeySwitch , and the bit length ( B ) of the 
small primes ( qj ). The hardware parameters include the 
capacity of SPM, the capacity of DRAM, and the num-
ber of function units, which are the number of groups 
in a tile ( g ) for the NTT unit and the number of lanes 
for the vector unit ( l ). The values of these parameters 
and their combinations profoundly influence the per-
formance and energy efficiency of FHE accelerators.

computational cost.

the parameter space exploration by requiring only the

The SPM serves as a cache to minimize access to 
DRAM. It does not cache data that is accessed only 
once, as this would not reduce DRAM accesses. In

Experimental setup
LP-HENN was evaluated using two homomorphic 
encryption convolutional neural network (HE-CNN) 
inference applications—LoLa-MNIST and LoLa-CIFAR 
(Brutzkus et al. 2019)—along with homomorphic encryp-
tion logistic regression (HELR) training (Han et  al. 
2019). LoLa-MNIST is a 5-layer HE-CNN designed 
for classifying the MNIST dataset (LeCun et  al. 2010), 
achieving an accuracy of 98.95%. LoLa-CIFAR is a 5-layer 
HE-CNN used for classifying the CIFAR-10 dataset 
(Krizhevsky et al. 2009), achieving an accuracy of 74.1%. 
LoLa-CIFAR is significantly larger than LoLa-MNIST, 
as its input has 3072 (32 Ã- 32 Ã- 3) nodes, compared 
to the 784 (28 Ã- 28) input nodes of LoLa-MNIST. Both 
networks conduct inference on a single image at a time. 
HELR compute a single batch of logistic regression train-
ing with up to 256 features, and 256 samples per batch.

Discussion
Performance bottlenecks and scalability limitations
LP-HENN primarily targets FHE workloads with low 
multiplicative depth, showing notable limitations for 
deeper FHE computations. These limitations stem from 
two main factors: the performance bottleneck of the vec-
tor processor and the scaling challenges in the number of 
crossbars in NTTU as multiplicative depth increases.
From a performance perspective, LP-HENN’s compu-
tational capabilities are constrained by its vector proces-
sor, Ara. Even at maximum configuration (16 lanes), Ara 
achieves a peak performance of only 33 DP-GFLOPS, 
significantly lower than specialized ASIC FHE accelera-
tors (such as F1) or GPU accelerators. This performance 
bottleneck cannot be addressed by simply increasing 
the number of crossbars in NTTU, as the fundamental 
limitation lies in the vector processor’s computational 
capacity.
Regarding architectural scalability, the number of 
crossbars in LP-HENN exhibits a linear relationship with 
the cryptographic parameter L . Consequently, support-
ing FHE programs with increased multiplicative depth 
requires proportionally more crossbars. This limita-
tion becomes particularly pronounced when supporting 
unlimited-depth multiplication operations. Such opera-
tions necessitate Bootstrapping to refresh ciphertext lev-
els. However, Bootstrapping not only incurs substantial 
computational overhead (involving hundreds of HMult 
and HRotate operations) but also demands larger crypto-
graphic parameters: N must be at least 32768, and L must 
exceed twenty. These requirements would necessitate a 
several-fold increase in the required number of crossbars 
compared to the current implementation.
Security
This section analyzes the security properties of the LP-
HENN architecture from two perspectives: the inherent 
security guarantees of FHE and protection against side-
channel attacks.

From the perspective of FHE security, LP-HENN 
inherits the security properties of FHE since it is purely 
a hardware implementation without modifications to the 
underlying algorithms. The architecture maintains secu-
rity as long as the application’s parameter selection meets 
the security level  requirements. A key security feature 
of FHE is that data remains encrypted throughout pro-
cessing—even if data leakage occurs during computation, 
only the encrypted form is exposed, preserving the confi-
dentiality of the original information.
Regarding side-channel attack prevention, LP-HENN 
exhibits inherent advantages due to a fundamental prop-
erty of FHE programs: their execution paths are static 
and free from data-dependent branching. Consequently, 
memory access patterns remain independent of input 
data, resulting in stable bandwidth utilization patterns 
that do not fluctuate with varying inputs. This bandwidth 
stability effectively mitigates side-channel attacks based 
on bandwidth analysis. Since bandwidth usage patterns 
remain constant regardless of input data, attackers can-
not infer any information about the input by monitoring 
bandwidth variations, thus fundamentally eliminating the 
possibility of such side-channel attacks.
Mitigation of ReRAM variability
As discussed in Sect. “Using array of crossbars to com-
pute NTT”, during RRAM programming, cell conduct-
ance may deviate from target values due to the stochastic 
switching behavior of RRAM, potentially leading to com-
putational errors. While conventional VMM operations 
in neural networks can tolerate some variation, NTT 
operations require stricter conductance control to main-
tain accuracy.
The error probability in ReRAM crossbars is primar-
ily determined by two device characteristics: the ON/
OFF ratio and device variation. A higher ON/OFF ratio 
and lower device variation correspond to reduced error 
probability. Research by (Park et al. 2022) demonstrates 
that when device variation remains within 0.005 and 
the ON/OFF ratio exceeds 200, the error probability 
approaches zero with optimal ADC quantization levels. 
Therefore, appropriate device selection and ADC quanti-
zation can effectively mitigate these errors. As mentioned 
in Sect. “Using array of crossbars to compute NTT”, to 
minimize error probability, we opted for smaller crossbar 
arrays (128Ã-128) and single-bit storage per cell.
An additional method for reducing error probability in 
devices with higher variation involves partial activation 
of crossbar rows. By setting inactive rows to zero, we can 
decrease the bitwidth of accumulated sums. For instance, 
with device variation within 0.1, activating only 32 rows 
simultaneously still maintains zero error probability. This 
operational mode is readily compatible with LP-HENN 
using either single-step or two-step recursive Cooley-
Tukey algorithms.
Conclusion
This paper proposed LP-HENN, a novel low-power, 
energy-efficient FHE accelerator architecture target-
ing power-constrained application scenarios, such as 
edge devices. Given the static nature of FHE workloads 
and the fact that FHE operations process long vectors, 
employing a vector processor is a natural choice due to 
its high energy efficiency. We present how FHE primitive 
operations can be decomposed into basic vector opera-
tions and provide RISC-V vector instruction descrip-
tions for these operations. Through the analysis of two 
HE-CNN applications, it is discovered that NTT is the 
primary bottleneck in terms of performance and power 
consumption. Since ReRAM crossbars are highly energy-
efficient dot product engines, LP-HENN offloads NTT 
computation to the ReRAM crossbars. To reduce the 
number of ReRAM crossbars, we adopt a decomposition 
method to compute NTT, which introduces additional 
element-wise multiplication. As ReRAM crossbars can-
not perform modulo and element-wise multiplication 
operations, we design a pipeline that enables collabora-
tion between the vector processor and ReRAM cross-
bars, allowing the computation time of crossbars to be 
overlapped. The design of FHE accelerators involves 
numerous software and hardware parameters; therefore, 
we develop a parameter selection model to automati-
cally determine the optimal parameter set that minimizes 
EDP. LP-HENN is evaluated using two HE-CNN appli-
cations, LoLa-MNIST and LoLa-CIFAR, and compared 
with a CPU implementation and FxHENN. For the LoLa-
CIFAR application, LP-HENN achieves a 31.82Ã- and 
11920.56Ã- improvement in performance and energy 
efficiency, respectively, compared to CPU. Compared to 
FxHENN, the state-of-the-art FHE accelerator with high 
energy efficiency for HE-CNNs targeting edge devices, 
LP-HENN achieves a 2.36Ã- and 10.04Ã- improvement 
in performance and energy efficiency, respectively.

Abstract: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables direct computation on encrypted data without decryption, ensuring data privacy in cloud computing scenarios and preventing the leakage of sensitive information. However, the compu- tational overhead of HE typically exceeds that of plaintext computation by 4 to 5 orders of magnitude, while energy consumption is 5 to 6 orders of magnitude higher. These substantial performance and energy overheads significantly hinder the widespread adoption of FHE. This paper proposed LP-HENN, a novel low-power and energy-efficient FHE accelerator architecture that leverages a RISC-V vector coprocessor and ReRAM crossbar arrays. LP-HENN targets power-constrained application scenarios such as edge devices, aiming to provide highly energy-efficient acceleration support for FHE applications. LP-HENN leverages the collaborative work of the vector processor and ReRAM cross- bars, employing optimization strategies to achieve full pipelining and minimize memory access. Furthermore, this paper proposed a parameter selection model for early-stage architecture design, which achieves an optimal balance between performance and energy consumption through the collaborative optimization of multiple parameters. Experimental results show that, for an FHE-based convolutional neural network (HE-CNN) inference application, LP- HENN achieves a 31.82Ã- and 11920.56Ã- improvement in performance and energy efficiency, respectively, compared to CPU. Compared to FxHENN, the state-of-the-art FPGA-based FHE accelerator with high energy efficiency for edge devices, LP-HENN achieves a 2.36Ã- and 10.04Ã- improvement in performance and energy efficiency, respectively. The energy efficiency of LP-HENN is comparable to that of F1, the state-of-the-art ASIC FHE accelerator, while featuring a low power design suitable for edge computing.
